nameStory: American burnweed gets its fiery name from its love of disturbed soil, especially areas that have been burned by fire. Like a botanical phoenix, this plant is often one of the first to sprout up in charred clearings and burned forests. The 'American' part distinguishes it from similar burnweeds found in other parts of the world.
description: American burnweed is a tall, weedy annual that can reach 3-8 feet in height by late summer. It has a single, sturdy stem with deeply lobed leaves that look somewhat like dandelion leaves but much larger. The small, whitish-yellow flowers are clustered in dense groups at the top of the plant and lack the typical daisy petals - instead looking more like tiny brushes. After blooming, the plant produces fluffy white seedheads that blow away in the wind like miniature dandelion puffs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small whitish-yellow flower heads in dense clusters with no petals - just tiny disc flowers that look like miniature shaving brushes, blooming from July through September

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed, alternate leaves that feel somewhat rough and smell slightly unpleasant when crushed - lower leaves can be 6-10 inches long with irregular, jagged edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single, sturdy reddish-green stem that grows straight up, often towering over other plants in disturbed areas by late summer

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white puffball seedheads that develop after flowering, each seed topped with silky white hairs that catch the wind

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hollow stems that often have a reddish tinge and feel firm but can be snapped with some effort - they may leak a slightly sticky sap when broken

habitat: Look for American burnweed in disturbed soils throughout New England - roadsides, construction sites, logged areas, and especially places that have been burned or cleared. It thrives in full sun and poor, recently disturbed soil where other plants haven't had time to establish. You'll often find it growing alongside other 'pioneer' plants like fireweed and goldenrod in areas recovering from disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of deeply lobed leaves close to the ground, often unnoticed among other weeds.
seasonality.summer: Plants shoot up rapidly, reaching full height by midsummer and beginning to bloom in July with their distinctive brush-like flower clusters.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to prominent white fluffy seedheads that disperse on autumn winds, while the plant itself begins to die back after the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stems may persist through winter, sometimes still holding a few dried seedheads, but the annual plant is completely dead.

funFact: American burnweed can produce up to 200,000 seeds per plant, and those seeds can travel over 100 miles on the wind - which explains how this plant can appear seemingly out of nowhere in freshly disturbed soil, sometimes just days after ground is cleared!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young goldenrod plants before flowering, but burnweed's leaves are much more deeply lobed and jagged (goldenrod leaves are usually just toothed). When in flower, burnweed's brush-like blooms are unmistakable - they lack the bright yellow petals of most daisy family plants.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this 'fireweed' with the much more famous fireweed (Chamaenerion angustifolium) that has showy pink-purple flowers. Many plants get called 'fireweed' because they colonize burned areas, but they're often completely unrelated species that just share this ecological niche.
compareHints: American burnweed is the only Erechtites species commonly found in New England. Among similar-looking daisy family weeds, it's distinguished by its combination of deeply lobed leaves, petalless brush-like flowers, and preference for recently disturbed soil. Unlike true daisies or asters, it never has the classic white or colored petals radiating from the center.
